entries.6120b56d37733714af024406bcfca78600e7e0d3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.1" sID="gen99704" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99705" type="x-p"/>We know that perseverance in prayer is a rare and difficult attainment; and it is a manifestation of our unbelief that, when our first prayers are not successful, we immediately throw away not only hope, but all the ardor of prayer. But it is an undoubted evidence of our Faith, if we are disappointed of our wish, and yet do not lose courage. Most properly, therefore, does Christ recommend to his disciples to persevere in praying.<div eID="gen99705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99706" type="x-p"/>The <hi type="italic">parable </hi>which he employs, though apparently harsh, was admirably fitted to instruct his disciples, that they ought to be importunate in their prayers to God the Father, till they at length draw from him what He would otherwise appear to be unwilling to give. Not that by our prayers we gain a victory over God, and bend him slowly and reluctantly to compassion, but because the actual facts do not all at once make it evident that he graciously listens to our prayers. In the <hi type="italic">parable </hi>Christ describes to us a <hi type="italic">widow, </hi>who obtained what she wanted from an unjust and cruel <hi type="italic">judge, </hi>because she did not cease to make earnest demands. The leading truth conveyed is, that God does not all at once grant assistance to his people, because he chooses to be, as it were, wearied out by prayers; and that, however wretched and despicable may be the condition of those who pray to him, yet if they do not desist from the uninterrupted exercise of prayer, he will at length regard them and relieve their necessities.<div eID="gen99706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99707" type="x-p"/>The parties between whom the comparison is drawn are, indeed, by no means equal; for there is a wide difference between a wicked and cruel man and God, who is naturally inclined to mercy. But Christ intended to assure believers that they have no reason to fear lest their persevering entreaties to the Father of mercy should be refused, since by importunate supplication they prevail on men who are given to cruelty. The wicked and iron-hearted <hi type="italic">judge</hi> could not avoid yielding at length, though reluctantly, to the earnest solicitations of the widow: how then shall the prayers of believers, when perseveringly maintained, be without effect? If exhaustion and weakness are felt by us when we give way after a slight exertion, or if the ardor of prayer languishes because God appears to lend a deaf ear, let us rest assured of our ultimate success, though it may not be immediately apparent. Entertaining this conviction, let us contend against our impatience, so that the long delay may not induce us to discontinue our prayers.<div eID="gen99707" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99704" osisID="Luke.18.1" type="section"/>
entries.d704a2521547f55fb149e41e54293f435c981f00: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.7" sID="gen99708" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7. </hi><hi type="italic">And shall not God avenge his elect?</hi> That <hi type="italic">judge, </hi>whom Christ has described to us as altogether desperate, as not only hardened against the contemplation of God, but so entirely devoid of shame, that he had no anxiety about his reputation, at length opened his eyes to the distresses of the <hi type="italic">widow</hi> We have no reason to doubt that believers will derive, at least, equal advantage from their prayers, provided they do not cease to plead earnestly with God. Yet it must be observed that, while Christ applies the parable to his subject, he does not make God to resemble a wicked and cruel <hi type="italic">judge, </hi>but points out a very different reason why those who believe in him are kept long in suspense, and why he does not actually and at once stretch out his hand to them: it is because he <hi type="italic">forbears</hi> If at any time God winks at the injuries done to us longer than we would wish, let us know that this is done with a fatherly intention—to train us to patience. A temporary overlooking of crimes is very different from allowing them to remain for ever unpunished. The promise which he makes, that <hi type="italic">God will speedily avenge them,</hi> must be referred to his providence; for our hasty tempers and carnal apprehension lead us to conclude that he does not come quickly enough to grant relief. But if we could penetrate into his design, we would learn that his assistance is always ready and seasonable, as the case demands, and is not delayed for a single moment, but comes at the exact time.<div eID="gen99709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99710" type="x-p"/>But it is asked, How does Christ instruct his disciples to seek vengeance, while he exhorts them on another occasion, <hi type="italic">pray for those who injure and persecute you, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.44">Matthew 5:44</reference>.) I reply: what Christ says here about vengeance does not at all interfere with his former doctrine. God declares that he will avenge believers, not for the purpose of giving a loose rein to their carnal affections, but in order to convince them that their salvation is dear and precious in his sight, and in this manner to induce them to rely on his protection. If, laying aside hatred, pure and free from every wicked desire of revenge, and influenced by proper and well-regulated dispositions, they implore divine assistance, it will be a lawful and holy wish, and God himself will listen to it. But as nothing is more difficult than to divest ourselves of sinful affections, if we would offer pure and sincere prayers, we must ask the Lord to guide and direct our hearts by his Spirit. Then shall we lawfully call on God to be our avenger, and he will answer our prayers.<div eID="gen99710" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99708" osisID="Luke.18.7" type="section"/>
entries.6189d0700ce590bfe1f3a3a4ec8cb13471b91e22:
8. When the Son of man shall come. By these words Christ informs us that there will be no reason to wonder if men shall afterwards sink under their calamities: it will be because they neglect the true remedy. He intended to obviate an offense which we are daily apt to take, when we see all things in shameful confusion. Treachery, cruelty, imposture, deceit, and violence, abound on every hand; there is no regard to justice, and no shame; the poor groan under their oppressors; the innocent are abused or insulted; while God appears to be asleep in heaven. This is the reason why the flesh imagines that the government of fortune is blind. But Christ here reminds us that men are justly deprived of heavenly aid, on which they have neither knowledge nor inclination to place reliance. They who do nothing but murmur against the Lord in their hearts, and who allow no place for his providence, cannot reasonably expect that the Lord will assist them.
Shall he find faith on the earth? Christ expressly foretells that, from his ascension to heaven till his return, unbelievers will abound; meaning by these words that, if the Redeemer does not so speedily appear, the blame of the delay will attach to men, because there will be almost none to look for him. Would that we did not behold so manifest a fulfillment of this prediction! But experience proves that though the world is oppressed and overwhelmed by a huge mass of calamities, there are few indeed in whom the least spark of faith can be discerned. Others understand the word faith to denote uprightness, but the former meaning is more agreeable to the context.
Luke 18:9-14
Luke 18:9-14
9. And he spoke also this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others: 10. Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. 11. The Pharisee standing
“Le Pharisien se tenant l’a;” — “the Pharisee standing there.”
prayed these things within himself: God, I thank thee that I am not as other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterous, or even as this publican. 12. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. 13. And the publican standing at a distance, did not even wish to raise his eyes towards heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, Lord, be reconciled to me a sinner. 14. I say to you, this man went down into his house justified rather than the other; for every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
entries.20e8020c0cbec5b3b1c20a096595f4340cd6d933: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.9" sID="gen99721" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99722" type="x-p"/>Christ now gives directions about another virtue, which is necessary to acceptable prayer. Believers must not come into the presence of God but with humility and abasement. No disease is more dangerous than arrogance; and yet all have it so deeply fixed in the marrow of their bones, that it can scarcely be removed or extirpated by any remedy. It is no doubt strange that men should be so mad as to venture to raise their crests against God, and to plead their own merits before him. Though men are carried away by their ambition, yet when we come into the presence of God, all presumption ought to be laid aside; and yet every man thinks that he has sufficiently humbled himself, if he only presents a hypocritical prayer for forgiveness. Hence we infer that this warning which our Lord gives was far from being unnecessary.<div eID="gen99722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99723" type="x-p"/>There are two faults at which Christ glances, and which he intended to condemn, — wicked confidence in ourselves, and the pride of despising brethren, the one of which springs out of the other. It is impossible that he who deceives himself with vain confidence should not lift himself up above his brethren. Nor is it wonderful that it should be so; for how should that man not despise his equals, who vaunts against God himself? Every man that is puffed up with self-confidence carries on open war with God, to whom we cannot be reconciled in any other way than by denial of ourselves; that is, by laying aside all confidence in our own virtue and righteousness, and relying on his mercy alone.<div eID="gen99723" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99721" osisID="Luke.18.9" type="section"/>
entries.e06fe1733e8517187fc8810e481b29ce90366018: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.10" sID="gen99724" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10. </hi><hi type="italic">Two men went up.</hi> Christ makes a comparison between the two men, both of whom, by <hi type="italic">going up to pray, </hi>seem to manifest the same ardor of piety, while yet they are exceedingly unlike. <hi type="italic">The Pharisee, </hi>possessing outward sanctity, approaches to God with a commendation which he pronounces on his whole life, and as if he had an undoubted right to offer the sacrifice of praise. <hi type="italic">The publican, </hi>on the other hand, as if he had been some outcast, and knew that he was unworthy to approach, presents himself with trembling and with humble confession. Christ affirms that <hi type="italic">the Pharisee</hi> was rejected, and that the prayers of <hi type="italic">the publican</hi> were acceptable to God. The reasons why the Pharisee was rejected are stated to be these two: <hi type="italic">he trusted in himself that he was righteous, and despised others</hi><div eID="gen99725" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99724" osisID="Luke.18.10" type="section"/>
entries.9eeab3ed3e74ea82b46749e2dd9bd09b8d615661: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.11" sID="gen99726" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11. </hi><hi type="italic">God, I thank thee.</hi> And yet he is not blamed for boasting of the strength of his free-will, but for trusting that God was reconciled to him by the merits of his works. For this thanksgiving, which is presented exclusively in his own name, does not at all imply that he boasted of his own virtue, as if he had obtained righteousness from himself, or merited any thing by his own industry. On the contrary, he ascribes it to the grace of God that he is righteous. Now though his thanksgiving to God implies an acknowledgment, that all the good works which he possessed were purely the gift of God, yet as he places reliance on works, and prefers himself to others, himself and his prayer are alike rejected. Hence we infer that men are not truly and properly humbled, though they are convinced that they can do nothing, unless they likewise distrust the merits of works, and learn to place their salvation in the undeserved goodness of God, so as to rest upon it all their confidence.<div eID="gen99727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99728" type="x-p"/>This is a remarkable passage; for some think it enough if they take from man the glory of good works, so far as they are the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and accordingly they admit that we are justified freely, because God finds in us no righteousness but what he bestowed. But Christ goes farther, not only ascribing to the grace of the Spirit the power of acting aright, but stripping us of all confidence in works; for the Pharisee is not blamed on the ground of claiming for himself what belongs to God, but because he trusts to his works, that God will be reconciled to him, because he deserves it. Let us therefore know that, though a man may ascribe to God the praise of works, yet if he imagines the righteousness of those works to be the cause of his salvation, or rests upon it, he is condemned for wicked arrogance. And observe, that he is not charged with the vainglorious ambition of those who indulge in boasting before men, while they are inwardly conscious of their own wickedness, but is charged with concealed hypocrisy; for he is not said to have been the herald of his own praises, but to have prayed silently within himself. Though he did not proclaim aloud the honor of his own righteousness, his internal pride was abominable in the sight of God. His boasting consists of two parts: first, he acquits himself of that guilt in which all men are involved; and, secondly, he brings forward his virtues. He asserts that he is <hi type="italic">not as other men, </hi>because he is not chargeable with crimes which everywhere prevail in the world.<div eID="gen99728" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99726" osisID="Luke.18.11" type="section"/>
entries.074fb3dabcd6c3d8fa24d30b1ec28d81309dbf55: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.12" sID="gen99729" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12. </hi><hi type="italic">I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.</hi> This is equivalent to saying that he performed more than the law required; just as the Popish monks talk loftily of their works of <hi type="italic">supererogation, as </hi>if they found no great difficulty in fulfilling the law of God. It must be admitted that each of us, according to the measure of the virtues which God has bestowed upon him, is the more strongly bound to thank the Author of them; and that it is an exercise of holy meditation for each of us to ponder on the benefits which he has received, so as not to bury in ingratitude the kindness of God. But there are two things here that must be observed: we must not swell with confidence, as if we had satisfied God; and, next, we must not look down with disdainful contempt upon our brethren. In both respects the Pharisee erred; for, by falsely claiming righteousness for himself, he left nothing to the mercy of God; and, next, he despised all others in comparison of himself. And, indeed, that thanksgiving would not have been disapproved by Christ, if it had not labored under these two defects; <note n="328"> <div sID="gen99731" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Si ces deux vices n’y estoyent, qui gastent tout</foreign>;” — “if those two faults had not been in it, which spoil the whole.”<div eID="gen99731" type="x-p"/> </note> but as the proud hypocrite, by winking at his sins, met the justice of God with a pretense of complete and perfect righteousness, his wicked and detestable hardihood could not but make him fall. For the only hope of the godly, so long as they labor under the weakness of the flesh, is, after acknowledging what is good in them, <note n="329"> <div sID="gen99732" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Apres avoir recognu le bien qui est en eux par la grace de Dieu</foreign>;” — “after having acknowledged the good that is in them by the grace of God.”<div eID="gen99732" type="x-p"/> </note> to betake themselves to the mercy of God alone, and to rest their salvation on prayer for forgiveness. <note n="330"> <div sID="gen99733" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et mettre leur salut en la confession de leurs pechez, et remission d’iceux</foreign>;” — “and to place their salvation in the confession of their sins, and forgiveness of them.”<div eID="gen99733" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99734" type="x-p"/>But it may be asked, how did this man, who was blinded by wicked pride, maintain such sanctity of life; for such integrity proceeds only from the Spirit of God, who, we are certain, does not reign in hypocrites? I reply: he trusted only to outward appearance, as if the hidden and inward uncleanness of the heart would not be taken into the account. Though he was full of wicked desires within, yet as he looks only at the appearance, he boldly maintains his innocence.<div eID="gen99734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99735" type="x-p"/>Our Lord does not, indeed, accuse him of vanity, in falsely claiming for himself what he does not possess; but it ought to be believed that no man is pure from extortion, injustice, uncleanness, and other vices, unless he is governed by the Spirit of God.<div eID="gen99735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99736" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> (<foreign xml:lang="el">σάββατον</foreign>) denotes in this passage, as in many others, <hi type="italic">a week</hi> But God never enjoined in the Law that his servants should <hi type="italic">fast every week; </hi>so that this <hi type="italic">fasting</hi> and the tithes were voluntary exercises beyond the prescriptions of the Law. <note n="331"> <div sID="gen99737" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Estoyent des exercises volontaires, et inventez a plaisir</foreign>;” — “were voluntary exercises, and invented at pleasure.”<div eID="gen99737" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99736" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99729" osisID="Luke.18.12" type="section"/>
entries.cc113beffe0d29a581828304832aac3528da9e64: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.18.13" sID="gen99738" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13. </hi><hi type="italic">The publican standing at a distance.</hi> Here Christ did not intend to lay down a general rule, as if it were necessary, whenever we pray, to cast down our eyes to the ground. He merely describes the tokens of humility, which alone he recommends to his disciples. Now humility lies in not refusing to acknowledge our sins, but condemning ourselves, and thus anticipating the judgment of God; and, with the view of being reconciled to God, in making an honest confession of guilt. Such, too, is the cause of that shame which always accompanies repentance; for Christ insists chiefly on this point, that <hi type="italic">the publican</hi> sincerely acknowledged himself to be miserable and lost, and fled to the mercy of God. Though he is a sinner, he trusts to a free pardon, and hopes that God will be gracious to him. In a word, in order to obtain favor, he owns that he does not deserve it. And, certainly, since it is the forgiveness of sins that alone reconciles God to us, <note n="332"> <div sID="gen99740" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui nous rende agreables a Dieu</foreign>;” — “which renders us acceptable to God.”<div eID="gen99740" type="x-p"/> </note> we must begin with this, if we desire that he would accept our prayers. He who acknowledges that he is guilty and convicted, and then proceeds to implore pardon, disavows all confidence in works; and Christ’s object was to show that God will not be gracious to any but those who betake themselves with trembling to his mercy alone. <note n="333"> <div sID="gen99741" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui tremblans a cause d’un vray sentiment de leur pechez, recourront a sa seule misericorde</foreign>;” —”who, trembling on account of a true conviction of their sins, shall have recourse to his mercy alone.”<div eID="gen99741" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99739" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.18.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99738" osisID="Luke.18.13" type="section"/>
entries.1219abee4e0985c1a37d7e4ef37fcdbc95dbe064:
14. This man went down justified. The comparison is not exact; for Christ does not merely assign to the publican a certain degree of superiority, as if righteousness had belonged alike to both, but means that the publican was accepted by God, while the Pharisee was totally rejected. And this passage shows plainly what is the strict meaning of the word justified: it means, to stand before God as if we were righteous. For it is not said that the publican was justified, because he suddenly acquired some new quality, but that he obtained grace, because his guilt was blotted out, and his sins were washed away. Hence it follows, that righteousness consists in the forgiveness of sins. As the virtues of the Pharisee were defiled and polluted by unfounded confidence, so that his integrity, which deserved commendation before the world, was of no value in the sight of God; so the publican, relying on no merits of works, obtained righteousness solely by imploring pardon,
“Seulement en confessant sa faute, et demandant pardon;”— “solely by confessing his faults and asking pardon.”
because he had no other ground of hope than the pure mercy of God.
But it may be thought absurd, that all should be reduced to the same level, since the purity of saints is widely different from that of the publican I reply: whatever proficiency any man may have made in the worship of God and in true holiness, yet if he consider how far he is still deficient, there is no other form of prayer which he can properly use than to begin with the acknowledgment of guilt; for though some are more, and others less, yet all are universally guilty. We cannot doubt, therefore, that Christ now lays down a rule for all to this effect, that God will not be pacified towards us, unless we distrust works, and pray that we may be freely reconciled. And, indeed, the Papists are compelled to acknowledge this in part, but immediately afterwards they debase this doctrine by a wicked invention. They admit that all need the remedy of forgiveness, because no man is perfect; but they first intoxicate wretched men with reliance on what they call imperfect righteousness, and next add satisfactions, in order to blot out their guilt. But our faith needs no other support than this, that God has accepted us, not because we deserved it, but because he does not impute our sins.

Luke 18:34. And they understood none of these things. What stupidity was this, not to understand what Christ said to them in a plain and familiar manner, on a subject not too lofty or intricate, but of which they had, at their own suggestion, entertained some suspicion! But it is proper also to bear in mind — what I have formerly observed — the reason why they were held in such gross ignorance, which was, that they had formed the expectation of a joyful and prosperous advancement, and therefore reckoned it to be in the highest degree absurd, that Christ should be ignominiously crucified. Hence we infer with what madness the minds of men are seized through a false imagination; and therefore we ought to be the more careful not to yield to any foolish thoughts, and shut our eyes against the light.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="18" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XVIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 ANd he spake a parable unto them, <ns0:hi>to this end,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 21.36. Rom. 12.12. 1 Thess. 5.17.</ns0:note> that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Duty of <ns0:hi>Praying always,</ns0:hi> is inculcated to us several times, in the Epistles as may appear from those Texts quoted in the Mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gint, which we must not interpret, as an Obligation upon us, to be always upon our Knees praying: for thus, our <ns0:hi>Obedience</ns0:hi> to it would be inconsistent with our <ns0:hi>Obedience</ns0:hi> to other Precepts of God relating both to Religious Duties and Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil Actions, neither was Christ himself always praying; but it either lets us know, <ns0:hi>that there is no time in which we may not pray, as we may pray in all places, every where lift<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing up pure Hands without doubting</ns0:hi> (as the Apostle saith) so we must pray <ns0:hi>at any time.</ns0:hi> Or, secondly, it is as much as <ns0:hi>pray frequently,</ns0:hi> and ordinarily, as <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Servants</ns0:hi> are said by the <ns0:hi>Queen of Sheba,</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>stand always,</ns0:hi> that is, ordinarily, and fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently before him, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 10.8. and the Jews are said <ns0:hi>always to have resisted the Spirit of God, Acts</ns0:hi> 7.51. That is, <ns0:hi>very often,</ns0:hi> for they did it not in every individual Act of their Lives, or else <ns0:hi>in every part of time</ns0:hi>: Knitting the Morning and Even<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing (the general parts of our time) together by prayer. Thus the Morning and Evening Sacrifice, is called the <ns0:hi>continual Burnt Offering, Exod.</ns0:hi> 29.42. <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 10.33. Or as it is in <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6, 18. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>: <ns0:hi>In every Season,</ns0:hi> when ever the Provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence of God offers us a fair Season and opportunity for Prayer. Or <ns0:hi>Mentally</ns0:hi> praying always, intermixing good and Pious Ejacu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lations, with our most Earthly, and Sublunary occasions; or, <ns0:hi>having our Hearts at all times ready,</ns0:hi> for Prayer, having the Fire always on the Altar (as was required under the Old Law) tho the Sacrifice be not always offering. <ns0:hi>And not fainting,</ns0:hi> which is the same with that, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.18. <ns0:hi>Watching thereunto withal perseverance,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.2. <ns0:hi>continue in Prayer, watching there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />unto.</ns0:hi> Not fainting either by reason of Gods delay, to give us the things we ask of him; or through laziness, and remission of our Duty, before our Life doth determine. This is now what our Saviour designeth to teach us in this Parable, which followeth.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Saying, There was <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>in a cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain City.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And there was a widow in that city, and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sary.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 6.10.</ns0:note> shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vertheless, when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?<ns0:note place="bottom">We have here the <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> and the interpretation thereof, both <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. in the <ns0:hi>Proparable,</ns0:hi> or the Words immediately going before it, and also in an <ns0:hi>Epiparabole,</ns0:hi> or some Words following it, which sufficiently explain our Saviour's Scope and Intention in it, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> To assure his People, that tho the Lord shew a great deal of patience towards Wicked Men, who are the Enemies of his People, and doth not presently answer their crys for a deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verance of them out of their Hand; yet if they go on crying to him, he will most certainly at length deliver them. To this purpose he tells them a matter of Fact, which either had hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pened, or might happen in the World. <ns0:hi>There was in a City a Iudge, which feared not God,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3, 4, 5. from hence he concludeth, arguing <ns0:hi>a minore ad majus,</ns0:hi> from the lesser to the greater, and indeed there is an <ns0:hi>Emphasis</ns0:hi> in every part of the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parison. 1. This was an <ns0:hi>unjust Iudge,</ns0:hi> God is a <ns0:hi>Righteous Iudge.</ns0:hi> He did this for a <ns0:hi>Stranger,</ns0:hi> Gods People are <ns0:hi>his own Elect.</ns0:hi> Then he assureth them, <ns0:hi>That God would avenge them speedily.</ns0:hi> We may from this Discourse of our Saviour observe several things. 1. That all the wrongs and injuries, which the People of God suffer in this Life, should make them fervent and frequent in Prayer to God for Redressing them. 2. That notwithstanding their Pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, God may bear with their Enemies long, for so much time as they shall think <ns0:hi>a long time.</ns0:hi> 3. If Gods People do not faint, but continue Night, and Day crying to him, God will hear them, and avenge them of their Adversaries. The Power that <ns0:hi>Importu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity</ns0:hi> hath upon Sinful Men, may confirm us in this thing, and ought to ingage us to pray without Ceasing and Fainting. <ns0:hi>Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vertheless when the Son of Man cometh, shall he find Faith on the Earth?</ns0:hi> When Christ shall come to Judgment, he will find very few whose Hearts have not fainted; there will be Multitudes who are fallen away, through the Power that Temptations have upon the frailty of humane Nature; by Faith here seems to be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood the true and proper effects of Faith, growing out of it as the Fruit out of the Rout. This Premonition of our Saviour al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so served for an excellent caution to his Disciples, that they would watch, and take care that they might be none of that part of the Stars of Heaven, which by the <ns0:hi>Dragons Tail</ns0:hi> should be <ns0:hi>cast down to the Earth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>as being righteous.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> that they were righteous, and despised others.<ns0:note place="bottom">By the Term <ns0:hi>certain</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>some,</ns0:hi> he unquestionably understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> and their Disciples, who (as we have all along in the History of the Gospel observed) were a Generation of Men, who were eminently guilty both of a <ns0:hi>Boasting of themselves,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>Scorning and despising all others.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publica<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>e.<ns0:note place="bottom">Who these <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and who the <ns0:hi>Publicanes,</ns0:hi> were we have had frequent occasions before to tell. The <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> stood upon an Hill; therefore they are said to <ns0:hi>Ascend,</ns0:hi> or go up. They had in the <ns0:hi>Temple</ns0:hi> set Hours for Prayer, as may be learned from, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 3.1. At which some of all sorts went up to pay that homage un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to God. Our Saviour mentioneth but two, having in it no further design than by this Parable to inform his Disciples, how much more acceptable to God, the Prayers of broken humble contrite Hearts are, though the Persons possessed of them be such as have been, or at least have been reputed, <ns0:hi>great Sinners,</ns0:hi> Than the Prayers of those who are Hypocrites, and proud, and come un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to God pleading their own Righteousness, in order to the obtain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of his Favour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 1.15. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 58.2. Rev. 3.17.</ns0:note> God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men <ns0:hi>are,</ns0:hi> extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publicane.<ns0:note place="bottom">From hence we may observe that <ns0:hi>Thanksgiving is a part of Prayer.</ns0:hi> It is said he Prayed, yet we read not of any one Petiti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on he put up. His standing while he prayed is not to be faulted, (that was an usual posture used by Persons praying) unless the <ns0:hi>Pharisee</ns0:hi> made choice of it for <ns0:hi>Ostentation,</ns0:hi> that he might be the better taken notice of: Which was too much their fault, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.5. whether the Term <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>with himself,</ns0:hi> in this place, signifyeth that he only prayed in his Heart, or with a Voice that could not be heard, or only that he prayed by himself, I doubt, for tho our Saviour, who knew Mens thoughts, could easily re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peat his Prayer, supposing it only <ns0:hi>mental,</ns0:hi> or at least with a Voice not audible; yet this seemeth not to suit the Humour of a <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risee,</ns0:hi> whose whole design was to be taken notice of, seen and heard by others he saith, <ns0:hi>God I thank thee, that I am not as other Men, Extortioners, Adulterers,</ns0:hi> &c. But was this blame worthy? may we not bless God for his restraining Grace, not suffering us to run into the same Excesses of Riot with other Men? Doubless it is both lawful, and our Duty provided, 1. That we speak Truth when we say it. 2. That we do not come to plead this as our Righteousness before God. But this <ns0:hi>Phari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />see,</ns0:hi> 1. Speaks this in the Pride of his Heart, in the justification of himself. 2. In the Scorn, and Contempt of his Neighbour. 3. Tho he were guilty of as great Sins as these, tho of another kind. In the mean time we observe, That he did not attribute this Negative goodness, of which he had boasted, or that <ns0:hi>positive</ns0:hi> Goodness, which he will tell us on by and by to the <ns0:hi>Power of his own Will.</ns0:hi> He gives thanks to God for them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:319" />12 I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Twice</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Sabbath,</ns0:hi> saith the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> but that is ordinary to denominate the Days of the Week, from the <ns0:hi>Sabbath</ns0:hi>; the mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing is, Twice betwixt <ns0:hi>Sabbath</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sabbath.</ns0:hi> Those learned in the Jewish <ns0:hi>Rabbines</ns0:hi> tell us, that the Jews were wont to fast twice in a Week, that is, the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> and Devonter sort of them once on the <ns0:hi>Second:</ns0:hi> Another time on the fifth Day (which are those Days which we call <ns0:hi>Munday</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thursday.</ns0:hi>) From whence some tell us that <ns0:hi>Wednesday</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Fryday,</ns0:hi> come to be with us <ns0:hi>Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sting Days</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Fish-days.</ns0:hi> The Christians in former times, think<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing it beneath them, to be less in these Exercises, than the Jews, would have also two Fasting-days each Week, and those not the same with the Jews, that they might not be thought to <ns0:hi>Iudaize.</ns0:hi> If that Custom had any true Antiquity, I doubt not, but they fasted after another rate, than the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> or others now do, who pretend a Religion to those Days. But neither was the <ns0:hi>Phari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sees</ns0:hi> Practice, nor the Practice of Christians in this thing to be much admired or applauded. For <ns0:hi>Fasting</ns0:hi> was always used in Extraordinary Cases, and the bringing extraordinary Duties into or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary practice, usually ends in a meer Formality. It is a good Rule; Neither to make <ns0:hi>ordinary Duties extraordinary,</ns0:hi> or rare. Nor yet <ns0:hi>Extraordinary Duties, ordinary</ns0:hi>; the doing of the first ordinarily issueth in the loss of them, and quite leaving them off; the latter, in a former lifeless performance of them. I <ns0:hi>give Tithes of all I possess.</ns0:hi> The Emphasis lyeth in the Word <ns0:hi>All.</ns0:hi> Others paid <ns0:hi>Tithe</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Apples,</ns0:hi> and some <ns0:hi>Fruits of the Earth</ns0:hi> (of which alone Tithe was due) but the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> would pay <ns0:hi>Tithes</ns0:hi> of those things, as to which it was generally held, that the Law did not strictly require them, such as <ns0:hi>Pot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />herbs, Eggs, Milk, Cheese.</ns0:hi> Our Saviour bare them this Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stimony, that they paid Tithe of <ns0:hi>Mints, Annis,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Cummin, Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.23. <ns0:hi>Rue, and all manner of Herbs. Luke</ns0:hi> 11.42. This <ns0:hi>Pharisee</ns0:hi> boasteth of his <ns0:hi>Exactness</ns0:hi> in two things; neither of which were required particularly by the Law of God. Nor did he amiss in them, if he had not omitted the weightier things of the Law, as our Saviour chargeth them to have done in both the Texts before-mentioned, but how came these things to make him a Plea for his justification before God? will he plead his <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> because he did things which God did not com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand him, whiles in the mean time, he omitted those things which God had commanded? Or, what did these things signify, if they were not done out of a Root of Love? The Law is, <ns0:hi>Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy Heart,</ns0:hi> and how could they be performed out of <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> when <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> was one of the things which our Saviour chargeth them to have o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitted? Of the same nature, are other Works, such as building of Churches, and Hospitals, and Alms-houses; the Fruit is good, if the <ns0:hi>Root</ns0:hi> be good. But if they be done out of <ns0:hi>Ostentation,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>opinion of meriting</ns0:hi> at Gods Hands, Mens Money (notwith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing these things) will perish with them, for Heaven is not to be purchased by our Money.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And the publicane standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.<ns0:note place="bottom">Those who fancy the <ns0:hi>Publican</ns0:hi> stood afar off from the <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risee,</ns0:hi> because the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> would suffer none but those of their Sect, at least none that were under such a Notoriety of dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />repute, as the <ns0:hi>Publicanes</ns0:hi> generally were, to come near them; suppose him to have been a Jew (which is not impossible) if he were a <ns0:hi>Gentile,</ns0:hi> he must stand so far off as the <ns0:hi>Court of the Gentiles,</ns0:hi> was from the <ns0:hi>Court of Israel.</ns0:hi> This <ns0:hi>Publican</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mility</ns0:hi> in his Address to God, is described <ns0:hi>by his Posture</ns0:hi>; he lookt upon the Earth, as one that thought himself not worthy to look toward Heaven. 2. By his Action, <ns0:hi>He smote upon</ns0:hi> his Breast, as one full of Sorrow, and trouble. 3. By the <ns0:hi>matter</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>form</ns0:hi> of his Prayer, he confesseth himself a Sinner. He flyeth unto the free Grace of God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Here's not a Word of Boasting, that he was not such, or such, nor yet that he did thus, or thus. He confesseth himself a <ns0:hi>Sinner,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Miserable Sinner,</ns0:hi> and fleeth to the free Grace of God, thereby instructing us how to make our Applications to God, disclaiming any Goodness or Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness in our selves, and fleeing to the alone Merits of Christ, and the free Grace of God in, and through him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 I tell you, This manwent down to his house justified <ns0:hi>rather</ns0:hi> then the other:<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 22.29.</ns0:note>for every one that ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />alteth himself, shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iustifyed,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, we Translate <ns0:hi>rather than the other,</ns0:hi> not that the other was at all justifyed by God, the other was justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied by himself only, and those of his party. The <ns0:hi>Publican</ns0:hi> was justified by God. It followeth, <ns0:hi>For every one that exal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teth himself shall be abased,</ns0:hi> &c. It is another of our Saviours Sentences often made use of by him, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.12. and in this Gospel, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 14.11. It is applyed to the ordinary pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice of Men, but hear to God in the ways of his <ns0:hi>Providence,</ns0:hi> he resisteth the Proud, and gives Grace to the Humble. The Blessed Virgin magnifieth God on this account, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.51, 52.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And they brought unto him also Infants, that he would touch them: but when <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> disciples saw <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> they rebuked them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 142<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 1 Pet. 2.2.</ns0:note> such is the kingdom of God.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="23">23 And when he heard this, he was very sorrow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful: for he was very rich.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And when Jesus saw that he was very sorrow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, he said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 11.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> How hardly shall they that have rich<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es enter into the kingdom of God.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="27">27 And he said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 32.17.</ns0:note> The things which are unpossible with men, are possible with God.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have met with this Story at large, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.16. And with (if not the same) very like to it, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.17, 18. See the Notes on both those places. The History is of great use to us. 1. <ns0:hi>To know how far a Man may go, that yet is a great way short of a truly good, and Spiritual State.</ns0:hi> He may know that nothing in this Life will make him perfectly happy. He may desire Eternal Life, and Salvation. He may go a great way in keeping the Commandments of God, as to the Letter of them. He may come to the Ministers of the Gospel to be further in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structed. But herein he will fail, He will not come to Christ, that he may have life, but fancy he should do something Meritorious of it, he doth not aright understand the Law, and that there is no going to Heaven that way, but by the perfect observation of it, and therefore fansieth himself in a much better Estate than he is. 2. It instructeth us in this, That there is no coming to Heaven by Works, but by a full and perfect obedience to the whole revealed Will of God. 3. That every Hypocrite hath some Lust or other, in which he cannot deny himself. This Rulers Lust was his immoderate love of the World, and the things thereof. 4. That it is a mighty difficult thing for any Persons, but espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially such as have great possessions on Earth, to get to Heaven. 5. As difficult and almost impossible it may appear to Men, yet nothing is impossible with God. He can change the Heart of the Rich, and incline it to himself, as well as the Heart of the Poor. The Rich Man hath more impediments; but be Men Rich or Poor, without the powerful Influenc<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of God upon the Heart, without his free Grace no Soul will be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>aved.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Then Peter said, Lo, we have left all, and fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed thee.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And he said unto them, Verily I say unto you, there is no man that hath left house, or parents,
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:319" />
or brethren, or wife, orchildren, for the kingdom of Gods sake,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Who shall not receive manifold more in this present time, and in the world to come life everla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sting.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.27, 28, 29, 30. and on <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.28, 29, The difficulty is only to reconcile, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. to Gods Providences. For the Eternal Life promised in the World to come, that is <ns0:hi>Matter</ns0:hi> of Faith, and not so much as seemingly contradicted by any Providence of God. But how many lose much for Christ, that in this Life do not receive Mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fold more, or an Hundred-fold. <ns0:hi>An.</ns0:hi> It is true if we understood it <ns0:hi>in specie.</ns0:hi> But the promise is not so to be interpreted. It is enough, if they do receive much more <ns0:hi>in valore,</ns0:hi> in value upon a true and just estimation. And this every Sufferer for Christ hath either; 1. In a Joy, and Peace, and assurance of Gods love, which is thousand times more. 2. Or at least <ns0:hi>in a contentation of Mind,</ns0:hi> with that State into which the Providence of God bringeth them; this also is much more, as any will judge it a happier State never to Thirst, than to have much Drink to satisfy the Appetite.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 16.21. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 17.22.</ns0:note> Then he took unto him the twelve, and said unto them, Behold we go up to Jerusalem, and all things, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 22. Isa. 53.</ns0:note> that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of man shall he accomplished.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 27.2. Chap. 23.1 John. 18.28. Acts 3.13. <ns0:hi>See the notes on these Texts.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully intreated, and spitted on;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And they shall scourge <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and put him to death: and the third day he shall rise again.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them, neither knew they the things which were spoken.<ns0:note place="bottom">We shall afterward in the History of our Saviours passion, see all these things exactly fulfilled, and our Lord here assureth his Disciples, that it was but in accomplishment of all that was pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesied concerning the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>; nor was it any more than he had told them, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 9.22. and again <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 44. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.17. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.32, 33. yet it is said, <ns0:hi>That they understood none of these things.</ns0:hi> The Words were easie enough to be understood, but they could not Reconcile them, to the notion of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> which they had drank in, they could not conceive how the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> that should redeem <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> should dye, or be thus barbarously used, by those whom he came to Redeem, or Save. We have great need to consider well what Notions we entertain concerning the things of God. All this Blindness, and unbelief of the Disciples, was bottomed in the false Notion of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> which they had taken up<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> However our Saviour thought fit to inculcate them, to prepare them against the offence they might take at them, when the Providence of God brought them forth, it is good for us to hear, tho it be only for the time come.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 20.29, 30, 31.</ns0:note> And it came to pass, that as he was come nigh unto Jericho, a certain blind man sate by the way-side begging.<ns0:note place="bottom">This blind Man was <ns0:hi>Bartimeus,</ns0:hi> the Son of <ns0:hi>Timeus,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> tell us, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.46. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentions two, the other two <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> but one, as being more famous, either upon his own, or his Fathers account.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="42">42 And Jesus said unto him, Receive thy sight: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17.19.</ns0:note> thy <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

               <ns0:p n="43">43 And immediately he recived his sight, and followed him, glorifying God: And all the people when they saw <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> gave praise unto God.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.29, 30. and on <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.46. where this whole History is more fully opened. It is here again very remarkable, how much Christ attributeth to <ns0:hi>Faith, v.</ns0:hi> 42. <ns0:hi>Thy Faith hath saved thee,</ns0:hi> which can be no otherwise under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, than of Faith, as the condition that was required in the Person to be healed, for it is most certain, that Christ by his Divine Power, was the Efficient cause of this Blind Man's healing, but he exerted this Divine Power, upon that exercise of <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> which he discerned in the Blind Man, whose Faith seemeth to be a degree higher than that of the <ns0:hi>Lepers, Ch.</ns0:hi> 17.13. who said no more <ns0:hi>Iesus, Master.</ns0:hi> Jesus, thou <ns0:hi>Son of David</ns0:hi> was much more than this. It speak the blind Mans persuasion, that Christ was the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi>; for it was an incontrouled Tradition amongst the Jews, that the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> was to be the <ns0:hi>Son of David</ns0:hi> Christ rewards the least Exercises of true Faith, but much more the higher Exercises of it. It doth not appear this <ns0:hi>Blind Man</ns0:hi> was fully informed, who the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> should be, <ns0:hi>viz. God-man,</ns0:hi> but so far as he knew he professeth, he calleth Jesus, <ns0:hi>The Son of David,</ns0:hi>
